improvement_notes: Reduce repetition across The Big Idea, See It in Your Head, Worked Robotics Example, Mini Simulation, and What Should Happen. The same edge list, winning route, and cost are restated many times, increasing cognitive load in a foundational lesson.

Explicitly state whether the implementation assumes comparable node labels. Python heap entries are tuples of (cost, node), so equal-cost entries require node labels that support ordering; the lesson currently presents the function as more general than this implementation is.

The Try It Yourself section presents a second, less-validated implementation that differs from the complete lab code. Either reuse the validated function or explicitly label this as a deliberately simplified variant and explain what validation was removed.

Clarify tie behavior when multiple routes have the same total cost. The B-to-D experiment produces a 7-second route tied with the original route, and the selected predecessor depends on strict relaxation and queue ordering. This is an excellent opportunity to teach that shortest paths need not be unique.

The generated engineering schematic's instruction to “trace the signal” sounds like language for electronics or control systems rather than graph search. Replace it with a graph-specific reading prompt about tentative costs, relaxation, finalization, and predecessor links.

The visual plan would be stronger if inline_01 showed one or two concrete relaxation steps rather than attempting to encode the entire finalized sequence and route in a single graphic. Preserve the exact edge list in text and use the image for one focused visual claim.

Move the additive-cost limitation earlier, immediately after introducing weighted edges. Students should understand before the worked example that edge costs are a modeling assumption, not necessarily independent physical travel times.

Add one short manual tracing exercise in which students fill in the next queue choice or predecessor update before seeing the completed table. The existing questions are useful, but most of the lesson supplies the reasoning before students must perform it.

The lesson is unusually complete, but its length and repeated caveats make it less efficient than it could be for Class 39. A tighter main path with optional engineering limitations would improve progression and retention.
